The authors must engage with the recent literature if they want to make credible
claims about benchmarking accuracy. Based on what is presented in Table 1 and the
papers referenced above, I believe the text: “Table 1 presents a summary of our
model’s training results, juxtaposed with existing state-of-the-art online and
offline SNNs. Our findings revealed that the models trained with our online
learning algorithms consistently and significantly outperform SNNs trained using
offline BPTT approaches and other online methods,” is not backed up by
evidence. Similarly in the abstract, “as well as achieves comparable or even superior
performance in neuromorphic tasks.” does not reflect reality.
Thanks for the valuable and detailed comment.
In the revised manuscript, we have reported strong performance on neuromorphic
datasets such as SHD and DVS Gesture, and have made the following improvements to
address your concerns:
1. Controlled comparisons under unified conditions
No. 2 / 22
We performed controlled experiments using a standardized setting across models,
datasets, and training hyperparameters, to isolate the effect of the learning
algorithms. Specifically, we re-implemented four high-performing spiking neuron
models (LIF, RLIF, adLIF, RadLIF) for SHD dataset, including those used in [Bittar &
Garner, 2022], under a unified training framework. However, we intentionally removed
certain components such as Batch Normalization that are incompatible with the
constraints of online learning. We trained them under strictly controlled conditions
- same hyperparameters, same data preprocessing, same hardware. Under these strictly
controlled and fair conditions, our ES-D-RTRL algorithm achieves training performance
comparable to BPTT, and significantly outperforms existing online learning algorithms
(see Table 1).
Moreover, following the suggestion of Reviewer #3, we re-implemented the EGRU model
from Subramoney et al. (ICLR, 2023) and evaluated it on the DVS gesture dataset. Our
ES-D-RTRL algorithm achieves over 97% accuracy on this benchmark, matching the
current state-of-the-art performance (see Table 1).
These new results, we believe, more clearly reflect the intrinsic advantages of our
learning rule in a realistic and practical online learning context.
2. Clarified wording in the manuscript
We have also carefully revised the wording in both the abstract and main text to
avoid overly strong claims. For instance, the sentence:
“Table 1 presents a summary of our model’s training results, juxtaposed with
existing state-of-the-art online and offline SNNs. Our findings revealed that the
models trained with our online learning algorithms consistently and significantly
outperform SNNs trained using offline BPTT approaches and other online methods,”
has been revised to (Lines 266-268):
“Table 1 presents the mean and standard deviation of classification accuracy over
at least three independent runs for each dataset. The results indicate that ES-D-
RTRL matches BPTT’s performance across most tested datasets and network
architectures.”
Similarly, the abstract now reads (Lines 15-18):
“Extensive evaluations across diverse SNN dynamics and computational tasks
demonstrate that BrainScale consistently delivers strong training performance
while maintaining extremely low memory usage and high computational efficiency.”
We acknowledge that some recent works, particularly those leveraging extensive
architectural optimizations, delayed learning mechanisms, and hybrid training
strategies, achieve higher absolute performance (often exceeding 90% on SHD or
significantly outperforming on DVS Gesture). However, many of these advances, such as
dilated convolutions, temporal attention, and adaptive delays, are are not directly
applicable to strict online learning settings.
Therefore, to ensure a fair and meaningful evaluation, we conducted an extensive
comparison in Table 1 against the latest state-of-the-art online learning methods
(including OSTL, E-prop, ETLP, OSTTP, OTPE, S-TLLR, FPTT, and OTTT), deliberately
excluding offline approaches such as BPTT with many architectural optimizations. This
allows us to better isolate and highlight the strengths of our proposed algorithm
within the context of online learning, rather than conflating performance gains
arising from architectural enhancements or offline training techniques.
No. 3 / 22
Comment 2:
Some parts of the paper are not necessary, including Figure 1 and Figure 2, which
has the additional problem that the underlying concepts (here called “alignPre”
and “alignPost”) are well-known in the simulator literature and are used across
modern simulator software (e.g. Brian, GeNN, NEST, …). This needs to be said and
relevant works need to be cited. Similarly, I would recommend that the Methods
section is reviewed and all parts that do not play a direct role in this work are
removed. In particular, the paragraph about dendritic computation (and the long
list of references with it) seems completely out of place. Also, many parts of
Figure 4 are more of an advert than a scientific illustration/figure.
Thanks for the suggestions.
We have carefully revised the manuscript in response to your comments, and made the
following specific changes:
1. Removal of Figure 1
We agree that the original Figure 1 was not essential to the main scientific content
of the paper. Its primary purpose was to help organize the narrative and clarify the
motivation and structure of the work. To improve focus and eliminate redundancy, we
have now removed this figure entirely.
2. Revision of Figure 2 (now Figure 1) and clarification of AlignPre/AlignPost
concepts
Indeed, the method of exponential synapses, referred to here as AlignPost , has been
extensively discussed and implemented in various simulators such as BrainPy, Brian,
GeNN, and NEST. However, the AlignPre abstraction has not been as clearly formalized
or systematically explored in the existing literature.
To address this gap, the revised manuscript now explicitly acknowledges this prior
work and cites representative references accordingly. Nonetheless, our main
contribution lies in tackling a critical yet often overlooked issue in the field of
online learning algorithms: the lack of a systematic summary and formal definition of
the model classes these algorithms support. For instance, methods such as OTTT are
limited to simple neuron models like LIF and rely on assumptions that do not
generalize to more complex neural dynamics. While more general algorithms such as e-
prop and OSTL exhibit some degree of model flexibility, their original presentations
do not clearly define the scope of supported network architectures and neuronal
dynamics. As a result, these algorithms offer limited guarantees when applied to
untested or more intricate models, raising concerns about their generalizability and
stability in practice.
To overcome this limitation, we propose a set of explicit abstractions  AlignPre and
AlignPost   that systematically delineate the class of neural network models
supported by online learning rules. This abstraction not only encompasses the
dominant spiking neuron models used today but also provides a formal foundation for
applying online learning algorithms to a broader range of network structures and
dynamic systems. The clear presentation of these model boundaries is a cornerstone of
the extensibility and generalizability of our framework, and it plays a foundational
role in advancing the application of online learning methods to complex neural
modeling and neuromorphic systems. Moreover, this formalism will offer valuable
guidance for the future design and refinement of online learning algorithms.
3. Removal of dendritic computation paragraph and associated references
No. 4 / 22
We agree that the section on dendritic computation was not directly relevant to the
scope of this manuscript. This paragraph and the accompanying references have been
removed for better focus and conciseness.
4. Reworking of Figure 4 (now Figure 3)
Thanks for the feedback that the previous version of Figure 4 was overly promotional
in tone. In the revised manuscript, we have substantially reworked this figure into a
more technical and explanatory illustration (now Figure 3). The updated figure
focuses on the hierarchical compilation mechanism used in BrainScale for online
learning, and clearly delineates how our approach differs from traditional BPTT-based
pipelines. The new version emphasizes how the compilation structure and system-level
insight enables the automation of online learning implementation, rather than just
advertising the software framework.
Comment 3:
The name “BrainScale” is very unlucky as it is almost identical with the well-
established BrainScaleS neuromorphic hardware which is well-known worldwide and
has existed for almost 20 years. This clash should be avoided.
We are indeed aware that the name BrainScale bears some resemblance to the existing
hardware platform BrainScaleS (brain-inspired multi-scale computation in
neuromorphic hybrid systems). This similarity has prompted several rounds of internal
discussion and exploration of alternative naming options. However, after careful
consideration, we believe that BrainScale remains the most appropriate name to
capture the core vision and technical essence of our system.
First, BrainScale is tightly coupled with the broader Brain Modeling Ecosystem (htt
ps:  brainmodeling.readthedocs.io/) we are building. This ecosystem includes tools
such as BrainUnit, which provides physical unit support; BrainEvent, which implements
event-driven computing capabilities; BrainCell, which enables biologically detailed
neuron modeling; and BrainState, which supports state-based compilation. BrainScale
plays a critical role in this ecosystem by delivering scalable online learning
capabilities, thereby completing the stack needed for advanced brain dynamics
modeling.
Second, the name BrainScale directly reflects the central objective of our system:
enabling scalability in brain dynamics simulation and modeling during training. The
term concisely encapsulates our project's overarching mission, supporting the scaling
up of brain-inspired computational models. Concepts such as "scale up" and
"scalability" are not auxiliary features but are foundational to our work. As such,
the name BrainScale clearly and efficiently communicates this core innovation.
Moreover, while the names are similar, BrainScale and BrainScaleS differ
significantly in scope and technological focus. BrainScaleS is renowned for its
contributions to neuromorphic hardware. In contrast, BrainScale operates at the
software and algorithmic levels, representing a fundamentally different layer of the
technology stack. This distinction highlights the divergence in application domains
and intended usage between the two systems.
That said, we deeply value feedback from the community and will continue to assess
the appropriateness and potential impact of our naming choices to ensure they do not
inadvertently cause confusion or undermine existing contributions.
No. 5 / 22
Comment 4:
Line 83: “Eq. 1 is capable of modeling the exact dynamics of realistic brain
networks under …” is unclear. Equation 1 is a discrete time approximation of a
class of neuron models that is usually understood to be defined through ODEs. In
what sense is it modelling the exact dynamics of brain networks? Besides, in what
sense are the dynamics of brain networks exact?
Thanks for the careful comment.
We agree that the original phrasing  “Eq. 1 is capable of modeling the exact dynamics
of realistic brain networks under …”  was imprecise and potentially misleading.
Our intended meaning was to highlight the consistency between simplified models (such
as those based on the AlignPre and AlignPost abstractions) and the original, non-
simplified dynamical models. Specifically, we meant that the simplified formulation
used in Eq. 1 preserves key dynamical features when compared to the original,
continuous-time models, thereby enabling faithful simulation under certain
assumptions.
However, even with such consistency, Eq. 1 remains a discrete-time approximation and
therefore cannot be said to model the exact dynamics in the strict mathematical or
biological sense. A more accurate description is that, under a given time step and
specific numerical integration scheme, Eq. 1 provides a numerically faithful
approximation to the solutions of differential equation-based neuron models. It
effectively captures the essential dynamical behavior of these models, but only
within the limits of its discretization.
Also, the term "exact dynamics of brain networks" is problematic in itself, as the
dynamics of real brain networks are highly complex and inherently uncertain. No
mathematical model can claim to capture them with absolute precision; all modeling
efforts are necessarily performed at a particular level of abstraction.
To improve the rigor and clarity of the manuscript, we have removed the old phrase
from the revised version. Instead, we now explicitly emphasize the rationale behind
the use of the simplified discrete form (see Lines 86-94) and discuss its advantages
more clearly (see Lines 95-99).
Comment 5:
Line 90ff : The concepts of “AlignPre” and “AlignPost” are not new and should be
referenced to the literature
In the revised manuscript, we have added appropriate references to acknowledge this
prior literature. Although AlignPost is widely recognized in the community through
its use in exponential synapse models, to the best of our knowledge, our work is the
first to provide a systematic formulation and unified abstraction of these two
classes of methods, AlignPre and AlignPost . We believe this structured presentation
helps clarify their conceptual distinctions and practical implications, and serves as
a foundation for more boundary-defined and extensible online learning systems.
Comment 6:
No. 6 / 22
Line 200ff: “To facilitate seamless integration of online gradient computations
with standard AD routines, we have made our online algorithms compatible with
reverse-mode AD in JAX by customizing the vector-Jacobian product rule. This
adaptation enables the online computation process to closely resemble that of
traditional deep learning models, requiring no more than two lines of additional
code (the red box in Figure 4F).” – unclear, how can a forward algorithm be made
“compatible with reverse-mode AD”?
By "compatible with reverse-mode AD," we do not mean that our online gradient
algorithm (a forward-mode computation) internally uses reverse-mode automatic
differentiation. Rather, we refer to the fact that we have customized the interface
of our online learning algorithm so that it can be seamlessly invoked via standard
reverse-mode AD tools, such as jax.grad . That is to say, by using familiar APIs
like:
grads = jax.grad(loss_fn)(params)
users can easily compute the forward gradients at time : . This compatibility
significantly lowers the engineering overhead for integrating our methods into
existing deep learning pipelines.
This is precisely what we meant by saying that "no more than two lines of additional
code" are required (highlighted in red in Figure 4F in previous manuscript).
We have removed this wording from the main text and revised the corresponding
paragraph to clarify the point and prevent potential misunderstandings (see
Supplementary Note L.3).
Comment 7:
Line 251: “However, without surrogate gradients, BPTT failed to train
successfully on this task, with its training accuracy fluctuating around the 50%
random baseline (Figure 5F). ” – unclear: how do you train using BPTT without a
surrogate gradient? What are you using for the non-existing derivative of the
Heaviside function? Is that a sensible thing to try?
Thanks for this question.
In our experiments on brain simulation models (Figure 4E–H, Figure 5), the outputs of
the recurrent layers are based on membrane potentials rather than spike events. This
contrasts with the brain-inspired computational models (Figure I–L, Table 1), where
the outputs are discrete spike trains. The main reason for this design choice is that
spikes are extremely sparse in realistic neuronal dynamics, whereas membrane
potentials provide richer and more continuous information, making them more suitable
as decoding targets in these models. Moreover, since it remains unclear how the brain
decodes information, we opted to use membrane potential as the decoding target
(Supplementary Note I.5). Nevertheless, decoding based on spikes can also
successfully accomplish this task, but converges slowly (data not shown).
Although the decoding is based on membrane potentials, neuronal spikes play a
critical role in the internal forward dynamics, since spikes are still used to
mediate synaptic interactions. Therefore, it is not a trivial thing that BPTT without
surrogate gradients cannot successfully train this tasks (as shown in Fig. 4F and
Fig. 5C).
No. 7 / 22
We have clarified this explanation in the revised manuscript to better articulate the
rationale that allows this comparison to be made (see Supplementary Note I.5).
Comment 8:
Line 267: “The capability of our online learning algorithms to learn long-term
dependencies raises important questions. The first is how our algorithms achieve
long-term dependency learning.” – awkward.
We have revised the sentence to read:
“We investigated how our algorithm achieves long-term dependency learning.”
to improve clarity and readability.
Comment 9:
Caption for Figure 6 E: “Sorted raster plot” – sorted according to what
criterion?
The spike raster plot in Figure 6E in the previous manuscript (now Figure 5E in the
revised manuscript) is sorted according to the timing of the first spike emitted by
each neuron. Specifically, neurons that spike earlier are assigned lower indices in
the plot, making the temporal structure of the spiking activity more visually
interpretable.
Comment 10:
Line 381: “Spiking networks have recently attracted substantial interest in the
field of BIC due to their superior capability to replicate the structure,
function, and dynamics of the human brain over traditional artificial neural
networks …” – a) define the acronym “BIC”; b) I don’t think it’s accurate to say
that neuromorphic computing was interested in SNN simply because they are more
similar to brains. (let alone the human brain!)
Thanks for your constructive feedback.
a) Regarding the term "BIC", we originally used it as an acronym for Brain-Inspired
Computing , but we agree it was a mistake not to define it upon first use. To improve
clarity and consistency, we have removed all instances of "BIC" and replaced them
with the more standard term "neuromorphic computing" in the revised manuscript.
b) We acknowledge that the previous wording was misleading. While the biological
plausibility of spiking neural networks (SNNs) is one motivating factor, it is by no
means the sole or primary reason for their adoption in neuromorphic computing. SNNs
offer several practical advantages, including event-driven computation, temporal
coding, sparse activity, and high energy efficiency—especially beneficial in real-
time and resource-constrained scenarios.
To address this, we have removed the problematic sentence and replaced it with a more
neutral and accurate statement (Line 256):
“Spiking networks have been widely used in neuromorphic tasks [3, 12].”
No. 8 / 22
This revision avoids overgeneralization and better reflects the multi-faceted
motivations behind the use of SNNs. Thank you again for helping us improve the
accuracy and rigor of our presentation.
Comment 11:
Line 470: “learn and adapt in real-time, ultimately bringing digital whole-brain
simulations closer to reality.” – there is nothing in the paper to suggest we are
close to whole-brain simulations. This sentence should be deleted.
We have deleted this line, and totally revised the Discussion section.
Comment 12:
Line 490/ equation (8): dv/dt incorrectly used for a discrete-time recurrence
equation.
We have fixed this typo.
Comment 13:
The code is not actually available I believe. The manuscript states only that it
will be available at certain URLs but I have tried them and they are not yet
accessible.
We have now made the full codebase publicly available at the URLs provided in the
manuscript. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the repository includes all
source code, documentation, and scripts necessary to reproduce the main experiments
and figures. We have also double-checked that the links are active and accessible
without restrictions.
No. 9 / 22
Response to Reviewer #2
We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and revision suggestions. We are
particularly grateful for the positive assessment of the proposed framework and its
focus on scalability, the appreciation of our architectural modularity and model
selection, and the recognition of the overall writing. Below we provide a detailed
response to each point raised, and we have revised the manuscript accordingly.
Comment 1:
I suggest organizing the numbering of the bibliography, e.g. according to the
order of use.
We have organized the bibliography according to the order of citation.
Comment 2:
Please verify the content of the Supplementary materials section. Not all of its
elements have links in the text, e.g. there are no links (and therefore comments)
to tables S1-S11. I suggest additionally increasing the font size on some charts
in this section, e.g. S12-S14. Please verify the notation in tables S3, S4, S8,
S9, S10, S11 with the values V_v, V_rest, V_reset, V_th (should be as in table
S7).
Thanks for your careful review regarding the Supplementary Notes section.
1. Missing links to supplementary tables (S1–S11):
The primary purpose of these tables is to provide a comprehensive summary of model
parameters used in the main text, serving as a reference for reproducing the
experimental results (although the source code can be a better way for
reproducibility). While we acknowledge that the tables are not explicitly cited in
the main text, their role is to complement the source code in supporting
reproducibility. Since one figure or table in the main text may correspond to
multiple supplementary tables, we chose not to add direct links, but rather to
present these tables collectively as parameter summaries.
2. Chart readability (e.g., Figures S12–S14):
We agree that the font sizes in some supplementary figures are too small and may
affect readability. We have revised Supplementary Figures by increasing the font size
of axis labels, legends, and annotations to ensure better clarity, especially for
print and screen viewing. Please see Supplementary Fig. S9-S11.
3. Consistency of notation in tables (S3, S4, S8–S11):

3. Exponential kernel vs. LIF dynamics
Regarding the similarity between LIF neurons and the exponential kernel in Eq. (7):
While both may involve exponential terms, their roles are fundamentally different. In
OTTT, the exponential kernel arises directly from the LIF neuron dynamics and is
tightly coupled to the structure of the neuron model. In contrast, our use of
exponential kernels in Eq. (7) is part of a generic temporal filter applied to the
output spikes, and is independent of the internal dynamics of the neuron model (e.g.,
LIF, ALIF, Izhikevich, Hodgkin–Huxley, etc).
Moreover, the influence of neuron dynamics in our method is captured by Eq. (8),
which models post-synaptic responses. This separation of spike filtering (Eq. 7) and
dynamical response (Eq. 8) allows our framework to generalize well across neuron and
synapse types.

The authors have made large strides in addressing the previous round of reviews. One of the main issues was to relate their
work to the recent literature on training SNNs on datasets such as SHD. The results of the proposed methods are now

This is a problematic argument to make. Fair comparisons are notoriously difficult, but in this case, the offline, back-
propagation-through-time methods yield trained SNNs with the stated performance and any normalisation with batch norm
during the training phase can be absorbed into weights during inference. So, in essence, there is no fundamental argument
against the use of batch norm. Removing it to make the comparison with a method that can't employ batch norm more

I want to thank the authors for the clarifications. The presentation has improved, but my main concerns remain.

proposed method, which is now presented as if it were original work.

Dear reviewers,
Thank you for considering our manuscript, titled as A general, efficient, and
automated online learning system for spiking network modeling, for publication in
Nature Communications . We are grateful for the thoughtful and constructive feedback
provided from all reviewers; your comments substantially improved the quality and
clarity of our work.
Over the past three months, we carefully addressed every point through substantial
revisions and comprehensive experiments. The attached, point-by-point document
details our responses to each comment. For ease of review, all textual changes are
highlighted with tracked changes in the revised manuscript.
Before addressing each comment in detail, we would like to summarize the major
changes in the current revision:
1. Learning performance and hyperparameter tuning: In response to concerns about
learning performance and unfair hyperparameter setting, we have conducted
extensive parameter searches on both BPTT and pp-prop methods using the SHD
dataset. We achieved a testing performance of 95.33 0.11% on SHD, demonstrating
the robustness of our approach.
2. Novelty compared to Marschall et al. (2020) : We have provided a detailed
comparison demonstrating how our methods differ from Marschall et al. (2020) ,
clarifying the distinct contributions of our work.
3. Clarification of "scaling" and "scalable" claims: In response to concerns about
potentially ambitious interpretations of these terms, we have carefully revised
the manuscript (including title, introduction, and discussion) to clarify the
three core innovations of our framework: a general , efficient , and automated
online learning system for spiking network modeling, rather than summarize them
as a misleading term "scalable".
4. Package naming: To avoid potential confusion between the names "BrainScaleS "
and "BrainScale ", we have renamed our package BrainTrace, highlighting its
focus on eligibility trace–based online learning algorithms for brain modeling.
5. Algorithm naming: Furthermore, we designate the algorithm as "pp-prop " (pre–
post eligibility trace propagation) algorithm to explicitly convey its key
mechanism based on pre- and post-synaptic eligibility trace tracking and
propagation.
No. 1 / 24
Response to Reviewer #1
Comment 1
The authors have chosen to rerun methods of competing works while removing some
aspects of their methods - most notably batch norm. They argue that this is a
fairer comparison of learning methods as batch norm is incompatible with online
learning, which is their own aim.
This is a problematic argument to make. Fair comparisons are notoriously
difficult, but in this case, the offline, back-propagation-through-time methods
yield trained SNNs with the stated performance and any normalisation with batch
norm during the training phase can be absorbed into weights during inference. So,
in essence, there is no fundamental argument against the use of batch norm.
Removing it to make the comparison with a method that can't employ batch norm
more favourable to that other method doesn't seem to improve fairness.
We thank you for raising this important point. We fully understand the concern
regarding the use of batch normalization (BN) and have carefully reconsidered our
experimental design choices in the comparative study.
First, we would like to further clarify why BN is fundamentally incompatible with a
true online learning paradigm during training. BN is inherently a mini-batch–based
normalization operation that depends on the global statistics (mean and variance)
computed over a batch of samples and across all time steps. This violates the core
assumption of online learning, which processes data sequentially and cannot access
future samples or global statistics. Therefore, BN cannot be applied in a strictly
online setting, and we intentionally excluded this component from our online learning
framework.
To comprehensively address this concern, in this revision we performed systematic
ablation experiments comparing the effects of different normalization methods on both
BPTT and pp-prop (see SI. P for details).
Finding 1: The effect of BN depends on the complexity of neuronal
dynamics
As shown in Figure S6, in BPTT training, batch normalization improved performance
only for the simpler RLIF network. In contrast, for more complex neuron models such
as RadLIF, BN actually degraded performance. This observation provides an important
insight: when neuron dynamics are sufficiently rich, the network can achieve strong
performance without relying on global normalization operations such as BN. This also
explains why our online method performs well without BN when using complex neuron
models.
No. 2 / 24
Finding 2: pp-prop achieves competitive performance without BN
In RLIF networks, we observed that with a properly chosen surrogate-gradient
function, the pp-prop online learner without BN can reach performance comparable to
BPTT with BN (90.1% vs 90.7%; see Supplementary Figure S11 vs Figure S6).
Moreover, as shown in Figure S6, even within the BPTT framework, the combination of
BN + RLIF yields lower accuracy than the RadLIF network without BN. This suggests
that increasing neuronal complexity may be a more effective strategy than introducing
BN. Our experiments further demonstrate that pp-prop benefits more from this strategy
and achieves better training performance under such conditions.
No. 3 / 24
Finding 3: Complex neuronal dynamics confer unique advantages for
online learning
More importantly, pp-prop shows a natural affinity for complex neuronal dynamics (see
Figure 4 for approximation accuracy evaluation in the main text). On the SHD dataset,
pp-prop combined with complex neurons readily achieves > 94% accuracy without BN or
data augmentation (Figures S9 and S11). In contrast, BPTT typically requires
additional data augmentation to consistently surpass the same threshold (Figure S8).
Conclusion
Overall, our intention was not to “beautify” online learning by removing BN, but
rather to present fair and transparent comparisons between two realistic usage
scenarios. The new experiments on the SHD dataset clearly indicate that BN is not a
prerequisite for high performance. With appropriately chosen parameters and complex
neuronal dynamics, pp-prop can achieve performance comparable to BPTT + BN while
fully adhering to the constraints of true online learning.
Comment 2

which also achieves competitive performance (without batch norm), such as the

representativeness of EventProp and (ml)GeNN in the field of spiking neural network
(SNN) training and simulation. In this revision, we have added a detailed discussion
of EventProp in SI. M and of (ml)GeNN in SI. N. Furthermore, we have included a
No. 4 / 24
comparison of EventProp’s best training performance [4] on the SHD dataset using the
RLIF model (see Table 1 in the main text).
1. EventProp follows a different training paradigm from this work
EventProp represents an event-driven, offline backpropagation algorithm. Although
its memory usage scales with the number of spikes rather than timesteps, it still
requires full backward propagation at each time step. In contrast, our work focuses
on online learning algorithms , which perform real-time, forward-only updates with
O(N) memory complexity, without backward time unfolding or full activity storage.
In practice, EventProp achieves roughly a fourfold improvement in memory efficiency
compared with BPTT on the SHD dataset [4]. However, our pp-prop algorithm typically
provides tens to hundreds of times higher memory efficiency (see Figure 4 memory and
speed evaluation in the main text).
Therefore, to avoid conceptual confusion, Table 1 primarily compares algorithms that
satisfy the online constraint, such as e-prop, OSTL, OTTT, and our pp-prop.
Nevertheless, following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have also added several
online/offline spiking models that achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance for
broader context.
Furthermore, the competitive results of EventProp on the SHD dataset are largely
attributed to extensive data augmentation and machine learning tricks, rather than
intrinsic superiority of the training algorithm itself. As reported in the original
paper, before these enhancements, the accuracies were modest -- ( for
feedforward and for recurrent models, Fig. 4 in [4]) -- slightly below
prior BPTT-based SNN results. After employing data augmentation and architectural
optimization (Section 2.3 of the original paper [4]), performance on the SHD test set
improved to .
To ensure fair comparison, we also tested our online learning algorithms under
similar data augmentation settings. We found that RLIF networks trained with pp-prop
achieved around 94% accuracy, demonstrating that our online learning approach
achieves even stronger performance under comparable experimental conditions.
No. 5 / 24
2. (ml)GeNN does not implement a general-purpose online learning
compiler
We agree that our earlier comparison of simulation frameworks omitted (ml)GeNN.
(ml)GeNN is a high-performance, GPU-optimized SNN machine learning library built upon
GeNN. It provides a high-level Keras-like interface that simplifies model prototyping
and leverages GeNN’s sparse data structures for efficient simulation. The framework
supports several representative training algorithms (e.g., e-prop and EventProp) and
offers excellent engineering value for rapid prototyping.
However, (ml)GeNN’s design does not address the “general and automated online
learning compilation ” that our work targets. From both its source code and
documentation, it is evident that mlGeNN’s training compilers currently support only
predefined neuron dynamics and loss functions. For example, the EventProp compiler
supports a fixed LIF hidden-layer model and a limited set of task types
(classification via SparseCategoricalCrossentropy, regression via MeanSquareError)
[2]; similarly, the e-prop compiler is restricted to LIF and ALIF architectures [3].
Thus, mlGeNN does not yet provide a universal compiler that can generate online
learning updates for arbitrary user-defined neuron, synapse, or learning-rule
definitions.
In contrast, our system is designed around a unified model abstraction and compiler
architecture, which can automatically generate online learning code for any spiking
network model under the same abstraction. This is the fundamental conceptual
distinction between our framework and mlGeNN. We have clarified mlGeNN’s functional
scope and design philosophy in the revised table notes (Table S2) and expanded the
related discussion and citations in the supplementary materials (Lines 1762-1764,
Lines 1811-1823) to ensure a more complete and fair comparison.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a promising paradigm for modeling brain dynamics and developing neuromorphic intelligence, yet an online learning system capable of training rich spiking dynamics over long horizons with low memory footprints has been missing. Existing online approaches either incur quadratic memory growth, sacrifice biological fidelity through oversimplified models, or lack end-to-end automated tooling. Here, we introduce BrainTrace, a model-agnostic, linear-memory, and automated online learning system for spiking neural networks. BrainTrace standardizes model specification to encompass diverse neuronal and synaptic dynamics; implements a linear-memory online learning rule by exploiting intrinsic properties of spiking dynamics; and provides a compiler that automatically generates optimized online-learning code for arbitrary user-defined models. Across diverse dynamics and tasks, BrainTrace achieves strong learning performance with a low memory footprint and high computational throughput. Critically, these properties enable online fitting of a whole-brain-scale Drosophila SNN that recapitulates region-level functional activity. By reconciling generality, efficiency, and usability, BrainTrace establishes a foundation for spiking network modeling at scale.

---

## Introduction

Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a principled route to modeling neural computation at millisecond resolution while retaining the energy efficiency and temporal precision that characterize biological circuits1,2. Yet learning in SNNs remains fundamentally constrained by the challenge of long-horizon temporal credit assignment: synaptic updates must depend on state trajectories that unfold over thousands to millions of discrete time steps. The dominant solution, backpropagation through time (BPTT) with surrogate gradients3–5, computes exact sequence-level gradients but does so offline, requiring storage of all intermediate states and thus incurring memory costs that scale linearly with sequence length T. For biological timescales, where one second may correspond to thousands of solver steps, this memory footprint quickly becomes prohibitive, limiting both the duration of trainable sequences and the size and complexity of SNN models6.

Online learning algorithms for SNNs have emerged as a compelling alternative. By updating parameters in a forward-only fashion, they restrict memory usage to a small set of per-time-step variables and avoid storing entire trajectories7. However, despite encouraging progress, existing methods have not achieved both model-agnostic generality and linear memory scaling simultaneously. State-of-the-art approaches that approach BPTT-level accuracy, including e-prop8 and OSTL9, instantiate large collections of eligibility variables whose memory and computation scale quadratically with network size, rendering them impractical for large-scale spiking networks. Methods that achieve linear memory complexity10–12 typically rely on restrictive neuron abstractions (e.g., simplified leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) dynamics) that do not generalize to the rich neuronal dynamics needed for biological fidelity. Most critically for practice, there is no analogue of modern automatic differentiation (AD) ecosystems for online learning in SNNs: users cannot write arbitrary spiking dynamics and expect the system to synthesize numerically stable, efficient, and accurate online updates automatically. The absence of such an automated, model-agnostic framework has hampered adoption outside specialized groups and has limited real-world impact.

Here, we introduce BrainTrace, a model-agnostic, linear-memory, and automated online learning system for spiking neural networks that closes this gap. This system provides a theoretically guaranteed, linear-memory online gradient algorithm for training general spiking networks, together with a compiler that automatically generates efficient online-learning code from user-defined SNN models. For efficiency, BrainTrace achieves linear memory scaling relative to the number of neurons while preserving gradient fidelity needed for effective training. For generality, this efficiency extends to a broad class of spiking network dynamics whose synaptic states can be organized along either presynaptic or postsynaptic axes. For usability, BrainTrace’s compiler automatically generates efficient online learning code for any user-defined SNNs, facilitating implementations across various hardware platforms, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), and tensor processing units (TPUs).

We validate BrainTrace across diverse SNN architectures and tasks. Relative to offline surrogate-gradient BPTT and online baselines with quadratic memory growth, BrainTrace delivers orders of magnitude lower memory consumption and high throughput, enabling long-horizon training on commodity accelerators. It attains strong training performance on standard neuromorphic classification benchmarks and brain-simulation settings, where it trains SNNs that reproduce neural dynamics underlying canonical cognitive tasks. Notably, BrainTrace scales to a whole-brain SNN of the Drosophila connectome15,16 and successfully fits whole-brain functional activity patterns17,18. In sum, BrainTrace provides a unified solution to general, efficient, and automated SNN online learning, paving the way toward large-scale, biologically grounded spiking network modeling.

---

## Results

BrainTrace supports a wide range of SNNs with the following discretized dynamics (Supplementary Note A):

|It = f(ht-1, It-1, It) and It = θ ⊛ xt, (1)

where ht ∈ RHd represent the hidden states of H neurons, with each neuron quantified by d state variables; It ∈ RH represent the synaptic currents; and t represent the timestamp; xt ∈ RI represents synaptic inputs (e.g., presynaptic spikes); and θ ∈ RP denotes connection weights between pre- and postsynaptic neurons (Fig. 1).

SNNs described by Eq. (1) are implemented using the AlignPre and AlignPost frameworks19,20 (Fig. 1; see examples in Supplementary Note B). Specifically, in AlignPre, synapses with identical parameters that share the same presynaptic neuron exhibit identical dynamical trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 8), enabling synaptic variables to be aligned with the presynaptic neuronal dimension (Fig. 1A). In AlignPost, when synapses feature exponential dynamics with identical time constants, multiple synapses from presynaptic neurons converging onto a single postsynaptic neuron are effectively represented by a single set of synaptic variables. This is achieved by combining the input to the postsynaptic neuron (Supplementary Fig. 8), allowing synaptic variables to be aligned along the postsynaptic dimension (Fig. 1B).

AlignPre and AlignPost decompose an SNN into two parts (Eq. (1)): (1) an “intrinsic dynamics” part that dictates the temporal evolution of neuronal states through the element-wise activation function f, and (2) a “neuronal interaction” part that converts presynaptic inputs into postsynaptic currents via the interaction operator ⊛. The decomposition can largely reduce computational complexity and memory consumption, enabling a simplified algorithm for SNN online learning (described in the next section).

BrainTrace achieves linear-memory online learning algorithm
The objective of SNN training is to find a group of synaptic weights θ that minimizes a loss function L that quantifies the discrepancy between target values and network outputs. When target values are provided at discrete time points t ∈ T, we compute the weight gradient by:

∇θ L = ∑t∈T ∂Lt/∂ht ϵt, (2)

where Lt represent the instantaneous loss at time t, ∂Lt/∂ht denotes the learning signal that arrival at the hidden state ht, and ϵt is the eligibility trace indicating how parameters influence the hidden state, which is computed as13:

ϵt = ∂ht/∂ht-1 ϵt-1 + ∂ht/∂θt, (3)

where the hidden Jacobian ∂ht/∂ht-1 = Dt + Jt consists of a diagonal matrix Dt derived from intrinsic dynamics f, and a square matrix Jt derived from neuronal interactions ⊛ (see Methods). The hidden-to-weight Jacobian ∂ht/∂θt captures the effect of weight changes on hidden states. Importantly, Eq. (3) imposes a memory overhead of O(H3) (Fig. 2A).

By leveraging SNN’s inherent properties (see Methods), we can reduce the complexity to O(H). Without loss of generality, we consider each neuron has only 1 state variable with d = 1 (but see Methods for generalized results for d > 1). First, we found that a diagonal approximation of the hidden Jacobian captures over 99% of the cosine similarity with the full Jacobian (∂ht/∂ht-1 ≈ Dt, Fig. 2B). This fact aligns with earlier practice8, which suggests that ignoring the gradient flow through recurrent connections in ALIF neurons does not significantly hinder learning performance. Second, we proved (Supplementary Note C) that the hidden-to-weight Jacobian can be decomposed as ∂ht/∂θt = Dt ⊗ xt, where Dt is a diagonal matrix with entries Dt,ii = ∂ht,i/∂It,i, and ⊗ represents the Kronecker product. These observations enable us to simplify the eligibility trace in Eq. (3) to:

ϵt ≈ ϵtD = Dtϵt-1 + diag(Dt) ⊗ xt, (4)

which we referred to as the diagonal-approximated RTRL (D-RTRL) (Fig. 2C). This diagonal approximation reduced the memory complexity from O(H3) to O(H2).

We further observed that ϵtD can be expressed as a summation of rank-one matrices: ϵtD = ∑t k=1 bt ⊗ xk, where bt = ∑i=k+1 diag(Di) ∘ diag(Dk) (Supplementary Fig. 9). Since inputs xt maintain consistent signs across time steps (whether as binary spikes in AlignPost or synaptic conductance in AlignPre (Fig. 1)), we proved that the sum of multiple rank-one matrices can be approximated as a single rank-one matrix between summed vectors (Supplementary Note D). Consequently, the eligibility trace can be simplified to:

ϵt ≈ ϵtD ≈ ∑t k=1 bt ⊗ xk, (5)

which still preserves a high cosine similarity with the full eligibility trace across LIF (Fig. 2D), ALIF (Fig. 2E), and other SNN architectures (Supplementary Fig. 15).

In summary, this approximation yields the pre-post eligibility trace propagation (pp-prop) algorithm (Fig. 2F):

ϵt ≈ ϵt f ∘ ϵt x, (6)

ϵt x = αϵt-1 x + xt, (7)

ϵt f = αdiag(Dt) ∘ ϵt-1 f + (1 - α)diag(Dt), (8)

where ∘ denotes element-wise multiplication, and α (0 < α < 1) is the smoothing factor corresponding to time constant τ = -Δt/ln(α). ϵt x ∈ RI and ϵt f ∈ RH represent eligibility traces tracking pre- and post-synaptic activity, respectively. The eligibility trace in pp-prop operates temporally, locally, and in an unsupervised way, effectively achieving memory complexity of O(H).

BrainTrace facilitates automated online learning compilation
The widespread success of ANNs primarily stems from the automation achieved in frameworks such as PyTorch21 and TensorFlow22 for their training algorithms, namely backpropagation and BPTT algorithms. To provide similar training convenience for SNNs, we introduced a compiler (Fig. 3A–E) that automates the translation of SNNs into efficient online learning implementations of D-RTRL and pp-prop, and subsequently deploys both models and generated algorithms across various hardware backends, including CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs (Fig. 3).

At the Primitive layer, the system encapsulates three primitives that capture the essential components of general SNNs (as formalized in Eq. (1), Fig. 3A). Specifically, Hidden State primitives represent internal neuronal and synaptic variables, such as membrane potentials and synaptic conductances; Parameter primitives denote trainable parameters, such as synaptic weights; while Connection primitives describe network connectivities, including dense, convolutional, and element-wise operations. By flexibly composing these primitives, the Complex Network layer supports the construction of complex SNNs with sophisticated dynamics and topologies (Fig. 3B).

The core innovation of the compiler lies in the ETraceGraph and ETraceAlgorithm layers. At the ETraceGraph stage, user-defined Python-based models are transformed into symbolic intermediate representations (IRs), which explicitly encode data dependencies between model parameters and neuronal states. The compiler analyzes IRs to extract higher-level computational graphs that describe how each model parameter, θ, influences the hidden state through specific connections ⊛. The resulting graph captures all critical information necessary for computing eligibility traces, including the hidden-to-hidden Jacobian (diag(Dt)) and hidden-to-weight Jacobians (diag(Dt) and xt) (Fig. 3C).

Subsequently, at the ETraceAlgorithm layer, the compiler automatically generates optimized online learning implementations based on the user-selected algorithm (Fig. 3D). The generated code includes both the logic for updating eligibility traces during state evolution (see Eq. (4) for D-RTRL and Eqs. (6)–(8) for pp-prop) and the gradient computation triggered by learning signals (see Eq. (2)). During this code generation process, the compiler also performs advanced optimizations, such as reusing shared eligibility traces within the same neuron population to minimize memory footprint, and vectorizing hidden-group Jacobian computations to maximize computational efficiency (Supplementary Note I).

Finally, leveraging just-in-time (JIT) compilation via JAX and XLA23, both user-defined models (Fig. 3B) and compiler-generated algorithms (Fig. 3D) are automatically deployed onto the target hardware platform, including CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs (Fig. 3E).

Through this hierarchical online learning compilation, BrainTrace provides a unified and automated solution for computing forward gradients (see comparison of Fig. 3F for BPTT and Fig. 3G for online learning) without introducing additional programming difficulties (see comparison of Fig. 3H for BPTT and Fig. 3I for online learning; Supplementary Note N). This end-to-end online learning system will greatly lower the barrier to entry for using online learning in SNNs, making advanced algorithms more accessible and deployable in real-world applications.

Algorithmic evaluations on approximation, long-term dependency, memory, and speed
We first assessed the effectiveness of BrainTrace compiled algorithms in approximating the gradient computation. Evaluations were performed over different spiking datasets (including IBM DVS Gesture24, Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD)25, and Neuromorphic-MNIST (N-MNIST)26 datasets), neuronal dynamics (ranging from LIF to ALIF neurons), and synapses (including Delta, exponential, short-term depression (STD), and short-term plasticity (STP)) (Supplementary Note B). We observed consistently high cosine similarity between the single-step hidden Jacobian (1/T ∑T ∂hi+1/∂hi; Fig. 4A) and long-range hidden Jacobian (∂hT/∂h1; Fig. 4B) compared to BPTT-computed Jacobian. Notably, high similarity values were especially prominent in networks with complex intrinsic dynamics, such as ALIF-based architectures (Fig. 4B). We further found that both D-RTRL and pp-prop achieved high gradient approximation accuracy relative to BPTT-computed gradients (Fig. 4C-D), validating their effectiveness for the gradient approximation. Moreover, both algorithms exhibited lower gradient similarities on N-MNIST (Fig. 4C-D), indicating some dataset dependence. Further investigation revealed several key insights about factors affecting the approximation accuracy (Supplementary Note G). Network size showed no significant impact on approximation accuracy (Supplementary Fig. 11). However, approximation declined greatly when either feedforward (Supplementary Fig. 12) or recurrent (Supplementary Fig. 13) weight strength increased to levels that produced unrealistically high firing rates. Additionally, deeper recurrent layers led to lower approximation scores (Supplementary Fig. 14), suggesting a preference for shallow network architectures in our algorithms.

We then assessed whether BrainTrace algorithms can capture long-term dependencies in datasets, a capability that is critical for effective SNN modeling. We trained recurrent spiking networks (Supplementary Eq. 73) on the delayed match-to-sample (DMTS) task27, in which the network is required to maintain directional information from the sample phase over a long delay period before making a decision based on the test period stimulus (see Methods). We found that while D-RTRL, pp-prop, and BPTT all effectively solve the task with surrogate gradients3 (Fig. 4E), only D-RTRL and pp-prop can learn successfully without surrogate gradients (Fig. 4F). We then investigated how our algorithm achieves long-term dependency learning. We found that both pp-prop and D-RTRL maintain temporal information through eligibility traces, but in distinct ways. In D-RTRL, ϵg responds to incoming spikes, increasing with each presynaptic event; ϵa captures slow Jacobian dynamics, enabling information to persist across delays; and ϵv combines information from ϵg and ϵa, remaining sensitive to input changes like ϵg while decaying gradually like ϵa (Fig. 4G). In pp-prop, the presynaptic trace ϵpre is driven solely by presynaptic spikes, while ϵpost,g tracks postsynaptic currents and remains constant; ϵpost,a and ϵpost,v evolves slowly, propagating long-term postsynaptic Jacobian information until learning signals arrived during testing (Fig. 4H). We also analyzed the differences in synaptic connectivity learned by pp-prop compared to BPTT and D-RTRL. pp-prop maintained similar weight distributions with D-RTRL and BPTT, yet it displayed distinct column structures, particularly in recurrent weights (Supplementary Fig. 21). Interestingly, similar column structures have been observed in the synaptic connectome of layer 4 in the somatosensory cortex (Fig. 3E in 28), suggesting that pp-prop may capture biologically relevant connectivity patterns.

Finally, we assessed the memory consumption and computational speed of pp-prop compared with other algorithms. Theoretically, for memory consumption, pp-prop requires only O(BN) memory, since it stores just two traces capturing pre- and postsynaptic activities, whereas other online learning methods demand at least O(BN2). Here, B is the batch size. For computation, pp-prop needs O(TBN2) operations for gradient updates but only O(TBN) operations for eligibility traces. In contrast, OSTL, e-prop, and D-RTRL incur quadratic costs for eligibility trace computation due to their reliance on matrix-based updates. Empirically, we ran experiments on the Gesture dataset to compare memory and speed of three training methods, BPTT, D-RTRL, and pp-prop, across different sequence lengths using LIF networks (Supplementary Eq. 70). We found that BPTT’s GPU memory usage grew linearly with time steps and crashed at 400 steps (Fig. 4J). By contrast, both D-RTRL and pp-prop required constant memory regardless of sequence length (Fig. 4J), with pp-prop being 35 times more memory-efficient than D-RTRL (0.5 GB vs. 17.5 GB). For computation time, all algorithms scaled linearly with time steps, but pp-prop ran slightly faster than BPTT and achieved a ten-fold speedup over D-RTRL (Fig. 4K). These memory and speed advantages were consistent on CPU (Supplementary Fig. 19) and TPU platforms (Supplementary Fig. 20). Additionally, we tracked model accuracy during training and found that all three algorithms achieved higher test accuracy as sequence length increased (Fig. 4L).

Performance evaluations on neuromorphic classification tasks
Spiking networks are widely applied in neuromorphic settings1,6. To assess the effectiveness of pp-prop for such applications, we conducted extensive experiments across three standard benchmarks: N-MNIST26, SHD25, and IBM DVS Gesture24. We evaluated multiple SNN architectures: (i) a two-layer RLIF network29 comprising LIF neurons with delta synapses and recurrent connections (Supplementary Eq. 70); (ii) a two-layer RadLIF network29 with adaptive LIF neurons, delta synapses, and recurrence (Supplementary Eq. 71); and (iii) a one-layer event-based gated recurrent unit (EGRU)30 (Supplementary Eq. 82).

Since performance depends on many confounders (such as data preprocessing, network architecture, and training schedule), we varied only the learning algorithm while keeping all other factors fixed. For each algorithm, we performed targeted hyperparameter searches to obtain strong settings (see Supplementary Note L). We report mean ± s.d. accuracy over at least three independent runs (Table 1). Across datasets and architectures, pp-prop matched BPTT on most settings while using an online, memory-efficient updater rule.

Against state-of-the-art online learners, including OSTL9, e-prop8, ETLP31, OSTTP32, OTPE11, S-TLLR33, FPTT34, and OTTT10, pp-prop consistently achieved the strong performance. Notably, on SHD, pp-prop exceeded the strongest baseline by more than 10 percentage points (Table 1).

Compared with state-of-the-art offline learning approaches, our pp-prop algorithm achieves comparable performance to the latest models that employ advanced architectural and training optimizations. For instance, on the SHD dataset, pp-prop even surpasses the best-performing models incorporating delay-based learning35. On the DVS Gesture benchmark, its performance closely matches that of models leveraging batch normalization36 and specialized neural dynamics design37.

Training excitatory-inhibitory spiking networks for cognitive tasks
BrainTrace is theoretically applicable to a broad spectrum of spiking networks, including biologically realistic circuits with complex neuronal dynamics. To demonstrate this, we developed a biologically-informed excitatory-inhibitory spiking network (Fig. 5B) incorporating: four-variable generalized leaky integrate-and-fire (GIF) neurons38 for complex neuronal dynamics, distinct excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) populations, conductance-based synapses39, and sparse connectivity40. Our network comprised 800 GIF neurons, with a 4:1 excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio and a 10% random connection probability, each featuring conductance-based exponential synapse dynamics (Supplementary Eq. 81). We trained this network on an evidence-accumulation task41, where animals navigate a virtual linear track and encounter seven visual cues (Fig. 5A). The task required animals to integrate left/right visual cues and, upon reaching a T-junction, select the corresponding direction. Correct decisions based on majority cue distribution were rewarded.

Our analysis revealed that when the readout layer decodes recurrent membrane potential dynamics for accuracy, both D-RTRL and e-prop achieved stable convergence on this task, whereas BPTT failed without surrogate gradients (Fig. 5C, Supplementary Fig. 25). Despite the network’s small size, BPTT required over 10 GB of device memory, and D-RTRL consumed more than 2 GB. In contrast, pp-prop maintained high performance with a memory footprint of less than 0.2 GB (Fig. 5D). Post-training analysis of pp-prop network dynamics revealed highly selective, temporally precise spiking patterns. During the evidence accumulation phase (0-1100 ms, Fig. 5E), sequentially presented visual cues induced orderly transitions between transient and clustered neuron population activities (Fig. 5F). Neurons in each population predominantly utilized a time-to-first-spike coding strategy for sensory processing. Notably, within each selective population, neuronal responses to external stimuli displayed clear rank ordering, with neurons firing sequentially in response to stimuli (Fig. 5F). Remarkably, these neural dynamics closely align with neuronal activities observed in the posterior parietal cortex of mice performing similar evidence accumulation tasks (Fig. 2a in ref. 41).

Modeling Drosophila resting-state functional connectivity via whole-brain spiking network training
The linear memory complexity of BrainTrace provides a crucial advantage for training large-scale spiking networks. To illustrate this, we trained a whole-brain spiking model of the Drosophila brain constrained by the FlyWire anatomical connectome15, to reproduce both resting-state whole-brain calcium imaging signals and their inter-regional functional connectivity17,18. Although the FlyWire connectome15 offers a detailed anatomical map of neuronal wiring, direct implementation of this connectivity in spiking network models16 fails to accurately capture either the resting-state neural activity in each neuropil (Fig. 6G) or the cross-neuropil correlations (Fig. 6K) recorded in experiments. We therefore trained the synaptic weights of the connectome-based network16 using our pp-prop algorithm.

We first converted the 17 minutes of calcium signals recorded from each brain region (Fig. 6A) into deconvolved firing rates (Fig. 6B), and divided the entire dataset into a training set of 80% and a testing set of 20%. During training, the network received the experimental deconvolved firing rate at time t (ExpFRt) as input and predicted the firing rate at time t+1 (SimFRt+1). The loss function was defined as the mean square error between simulated and experimental firing rates. The pp-prop algorithm then continuously adjusted synaptic weights online according to the error gradients, enabling the network to autonomously learn the complex spatiotemporal patterns underlying resting state dynamics. This model consumes approximately 8.9 GB of GPU memory with pp-prop, and the loss converges slowly over epochs (Fig. 6D). In contrast, training with D-RTRL and BPTT exceeds the 32 GB capacity of a single GPU (Supplementary Fig. 24).

At the neuropil level, we evaluated the model’s dynamics in the mushroom body to assess training-induced improvements (Fig. 6E–G). In the warmup phase, we initialized whole-brain dynamics by feeding the first 84 seconds of experimental firing rates into the model; thereafter, without external inputs, the model generated ongoing neural activity solely from its previous timestep’s neuropil state. Before training, the model failed to reproduce any experimentally observed spontaneous fluctuations (Fig. 6G); after training, however, its output not only exhibited activation patterns highly consistent with the experimental recordings ("Train” phase in Fig. 6F) but also sustained similar oscillation patterns on previously novel test data ("Test” phase in Fig. 6F). These results demonstrate the model’s ability to generalize to untrained neural dynamics. To quantify improvements in all brain regions across the entire Drosophila brain, we computed Pearson correlations between model-generated and experimental firing rates for each of 68 regions, both pre- and post-training. Training produced a marked uplift in regional fit, and statistical tests confirmed that nearly every region exhibited a significant post-training correlation increase (Fig. 6H).

At the whole-brain level, we further compared whole-brain functional connectivity among experimental recordings, the untrained model’s spontaneous activity, and the trained model’s output (Fig. 6I–K). Prior to training, neurons within each neuropil exhibited spontaneous fluctuations with similar activity patterns (Supplementary Fig. 22), leading to high correlations across neuropils (Fig. 6K). After training, the model dynamics generated highly consistent functional connectivity strengths and patterns (Fig. 6J and Supplementary Fig. 23) compared to experimental data, regardless of whether during the training or testing phases.
