## Methods

Inspecting inherent properties of spiking networks
Property 1: intrinsic neuronal dynamics dominate the hidden Jacobian. A typical SNN exhibit two types of recurrent connections. The first type comprises Dt recurrent spiking connections that propagate action potentials between neurons (see ⊛ in Eq. (1) and examples in Supplementary Note B). The second type Jt consists of intrinsic neuronal dynamics, such as leaky terms in neuronal and synaptic processes (see f Eq. (1) and examples in Supplementary Note B). As a result, the hidden Jacobian is composed of two parts: ∂ht/∂ht-1 = Dt + Jt, where Dt ∈ RH×H is a diagonal matrix resulting from the element-wise intrinsic dynamics, and Jt is the square matrix derived from the recurrent spiking connections. Dt is actually a block diagonal matrix of dimensions RHd×Hd, consisting of H-by-H blocks. Each diagonal block, Dt,ii, is a d-by-d square matrix, where d is the number of state variables aligned to neuron i. For example, refer to Supplementary Note B. Without loss of generality, all subsequent derivations assumed = 1, making Dt a diagonal matrix of dimensions RH×H.

A defining characteristic of SNNs is their sparse activation patterns, with neurons firing at relatively low frequencies. Empirical studies have shown that biological neurons typically emit between 0.2 and 5 spikes per second42, with only 1–2% of neurons in a cortical network active at any given moment43,50. This fact leads to the hypothesis that Jt exerts limited influence and can be ignored in the hidden Jacobian, since Jt is highly sparse in both space and time. Earlier practices, such as e-prop8 and RFLO51, have also demonstrated that neglecting the gradient flow through recurrent spiking connections in specific neuronal dynamics does not significantly hinder learning performance. To further validate this hypothesis, we conducted empirical evaluations across various SNN architectures with different neuronal and synaptic dynamics (Supplementary Note B). Our findings consistently indicated that the hidden Jacobian of most SNNs is predominantly shaped by the diagonal Jacobian Dt induced by intrinsic dynamics. The diagonal approximation demonstrates a remarkably high cosine similarity with the full hidden Jacobian (see Fig. 2B). Notably, under biologically plausible firing regimes (fraction of spiking neurons <10%), the cosine similarity exceeds 99%.

Proposition 1. In sparsely activated SNNs, the hidden Jacobian ∂ht/∂ht-1 is dominated by the diagonal Jacobian Dt induced by intrinsic neural dynamics. This can be expressed as:

∂ht/∂ht-1 ≈ Dt. (9)

Property 2: physical connections yield decomposable hidden-to-weight Jacobian. Biological SNNs are characterized by physically constrained connections, reflecting the actual synaptic formations between pre- and postsynaptic neurons. Specifically, in AlignPre and AlignPost abstractions, this structural property can be mathematically expressed as a parameterized transformation from inputs to hidden vectors, followed by the element-wise activation applied to the resulting hidden vectors (see Eq. (1)). Such mathematical operation leads to an important implication: the hidden-to-weight Jacobian ∂ht/∂θt, which quantifies the sensitivity of the network’s output to changes in synaptic weights, can be decomposed into a Kronecker product of a vector and a diagonal matrix (see Theorem 2 and its proof in Supplementary Note C; this observation has also been illustrated in ref. 52 for rate-based recurrent neural networks).

Theorem 2. Given Eq. (1), let It = θ ⊛ xt, then the gradient of ht with respect to θ at time t is

∂ht/∂θt = Dt ⊗ xt, (10)

where Dt is a diagonal matrix with ∂ht,i/∂It,i as its diagonal entry Dt,ii, and ⊗ is the Kronecker product.

Dt is actually a block diagonal matrix of dimensions RHd×H, consisting of H-by-H blocks. Each diagonal block, Dt,ii, is a d-by-1 matrix. For example, refer to Supplementary Note B. With loss of generality, all subsequent derivations assume d = 1, making Dt a diagonal matrix of dimensions RH×H.

Property 3: sign-preserving neuronal outputs induce low-rank structure. Another unique characteristic of SNNs is that the outputs of each neuron, corresponding to inputs xt, maintain a consistent sign across all time steps. For AlignPost projections, x denotes the binary spike vector (see Supplementary Eq. 63, 64); while for AlignPre projections, xt denotes the synaptic conductance (see Supplementary Eq. 61, 62). In both cases, the elements in xt are sign-preserving and consistently positive across all time steps. Additionally, for the monotonous activation function f, its derivative Dt also maintains a consistent sign throughout all times. This distinctive property leads to an important mathematical implication: the summation of multiple rank-one matrices can be approximated by the rank-one outer product of the summed vectors. Theorem 3 formalizes this concept, with its theoretical proof presented in Supplementary Note D and empirical validation on various spiking dynamics using real-world neuromorphic datasets provided in Supplementary Note F.

Theorem 3. Let a ∈ Rm and b ∈ Rn be vectors where all elements in ai and bi are of the same sign (i.e., they are all positive or negative). Then the cosine similarity between ∑r i=1 ai ⊗ bi and (∑r i=1 ai) ⊗ (∑r i=1 bi) approaches 1 as r → ∞:

lim r→∞ cos(∑r i=1 ai ⊗ bi, (∑r i=1 ai) ⊗ (∑r i=1 bi)) = 1. (11)

Derivation of online learning algorithms
Theoretical basics of RTRL. Let us consider biological SNNs whose dynamics are governed by Eq. (1). At each time step t ∈ T, we assume the objective is to optimize the loss L = ∑t Lt with respect to the parameters θ, utilizing the gradient

∇θ L = ∑t∈T ∂Lt/∂θt = ∑t∈T ∑k=1 t ∂Lt/∂ht ∂ht/∂hk ∂hk/∂θk, (12)

where θk represents the parameters utilized at time t, ∂Lt/∂ht ∂ht/∂hk measures how θ at step k affects the loss at step t≥k, and ∂ht/∂hk transports the error through time from step t to step k. When k ≪ t, the transport captures a long-term dependency; otherwise, a short-term dependency.

To compute Eq. (12), two methods are commonly used, that is BPTT and RTRL13, which iteratively perform the error propagation on the unfolded computation graph through time backwardly and forwardly, respectively (also refer to Supplementary Fig. 16). For the RTRL, the gradient is updated in the forward direction:

∇θ L = ∑t∈T ∂Lt/∂ht ϵt, (13)

ϵt = ∂ht/∂ht-1 ϵt-1 + ∂ht/∂θt, (14)

where the eligibility trace ϵt ∈ RH×H×I calculates the effect of the parameters ϵt. To better illustrate the difference between BPTT and RTRL, let’s examine the gradients of the loss at time t with respect to the parameter at time k, denoted as ∂Lt/∂θk, where t≥k. Supplementary Fig. 16 demonstrates that BPTT’s backward computation of gradients is significantly more efficient than RTRL’s forward computation. This is because the product of Jacobians from the end to the beginning of the composed function only requires O(H) memory storage. In contrast, RTRL’s memory complexity is O(H×H×I) as it computes Jacobian products forwardly. To reduce the intrinsic complexity of RTRL, we should take full consideration of SNN properties.

Derivation of the D-RTRL algorithm from RTRL. In the following, we concentrate on the scenario where the hidden state dimension d = 1 to develop the D-RTRL algorithm.

As stated above, the raw RTRL has a high memory complexity. By substituting Eqs. (9) and (10) into Eq. (14), we can approximate ϵt as:

ϵt ≈ Dt ϵt-1 + Dt ⊗ xt, (15)

Eq. (15) results in a very sparse matrix with O(H×H×I) memory complexity. For compact storage, the above equation is equivalent to the following form:

ϵt ≈ Dtϵt-1 + diag(Dt) ⊗ xt, (16)

where diag(Dt) ∈ RH is the vector storing the diagonal elements of Dt. This results in ϵt having the shape of RH×I.

In practice, Dt is stored as a vector diag(Dt) ∈ RH×1. Consequently, Eq. (16) can be reformulated using element-wise multiplication. Combining with Eq. (13), we can express the learning rule of the D-RTRL algorithm as:

∇θ Lt ≈ ∂Lt/∂ht diag(Dt) ϵt-1 + diag(Dt) ⊗ xt, (17)

where the D-RTRL algorithm is a memory-efficient approach that avoids the O(H3) complexity of RTRL. This efficiency scaling arises because the eligibility trace ϵt only stores historical information for each active synaptic connection. In sparse neural networks, D-RTRL achieves additional memory savings by eliminating traces for zero-weight connections. Convolutional layers further benefit from this approach, as their parameter count is typically smaller than the number of pre- and postsynaptic neurons when using small kernels.

Derivation of the pp-prop algorithm from D-RTRL. Given the learning rule of the D-RTRL algorithm in Eq. (17), let’s consider the influence of θ at step k to the loss Lt at step t (t≥k). It can be approximated by:

∂Lt/∂θk ≈ ∂Lt/∂ht (Dt ⊗ xk), (18)

Therefore, at the time t, the parameter gradient accumulated up to time t has the form of:

∇θ Lt = ∑t k=1 ∂Lt/∂ht (Di ⊗ Dk ⊗ xk), (19)

Here, we assume that a learning target is provided at each time step k ∈ [1,⋯ ,t]. Moreover, ∂Lt/∂ht ∈ RH is defined as a row vector in Eqs. (18) and (19).

Since Di and Dk are diagonal matrices, we can only keep their diagonal elements as vectors, and their matrix multiplication operations are equivalent to the element-wise Hadamard products of diagonal vectors:

∇θ Lt ≈ ∂Lt/∂ht (diag(Dt) ∘ diag(Dt-1) ∘ diag(Dk+1) ∘ diag(Dk) ⊗ xk), (20)

Equation (20) results in significant memory overhead because the summation requires storing t pairs of vectors representing pre- and postsynaptic activity. This memory requirement is equivalent to BPTT, with complexity scaling linearly as time progresses.

We found a solution to this issue by fully leveraging the unique properties of SNNs. The key insight lies in the nature of neuronal output of SNNs: (1) Binary events: neurons in SNNs output binary signals (spikes); (2) Non-negativity: these spike events are always non-negative (see Theorem 3). This theorem allows us to approximate Eq. (20) by

∇θ Lt ≈ ∂Lt/∂ht (∑t k=1 bt ⊗ xk), (21)

where bt = diag(Dt) ∘ ⋯ ∘ diag(Dk+1) ∘ diag(Dk).

To avoid the exploding problem, the eligibility trace should prioritize recent activities rather than retain a complete historical record over a very long sequence. We implemented this by modifying Eq. (21) using two key techniques: exponential smoothing for bt and a low-pass filter for x. The former computes a running average of bt online, while the latter calculates a running summation of x. These adaptations form the foundation of our pp-prop algorithm, whose learning rule can be expressed as follows:

∇θ L ≈ ∑t=T ∂Lt/∂ht ∘ ϵt f ⊗ ϵt x, (22)

ϵt x = αϵt-1 x + xt,

ϵt f = αdiag(Dt) ∘ ϵt-1 f + (1 - α)diag(Dt),

where α (0 < α < 1) is the smoothing factor, corresponding to the time constant τ = -Δt/ln(α).

Generalization to hidden states with multiple variables (d > 1). The derivations above assumed d = 1, but generalize straightforwardly to d > 1. When d > 1, the matrices transform into block structures as follows (see examples in Supplementary Note B):

(cid:129) ht ∈ RHd×1: A block vector with H blocks of shape Rd×1, where block i contains the state variables of neuron i.

(cid:129) Dt ∈ RHd×Hd: A block diagonal matrix with H diagonal blocks of shape d×d, where Dt,ii is the Jacobian between state variables of neuron i.

(cid:129) Dt f ∈ RHd×H: A block diagonal matrix with H diagonal blocks of shape d×1, where Dt,ii = ∂ht,i/∂It,i.

(cid:129) ∂Lt/∂ht ∈ RHd×1: A block vector with H blocks of shape Rd×1.

The online learning framework in Eqs. (17) and (22) remain unchanged; only the ∘ operation differs. For d = 1, ∘ denotes element-wise scalar multiplication. For d > 1, ∘ it becomes block-wise multiplication, where each block undergoes d-dimensional matrix or inner product operations.

To illustrate, consider the learning rule for a single weight θji connecting neurons i and j. For D-RTRL, Eq. (17) becomes:

∇θ ji L ≈ ∑t∈T ∂Lt/∂ht,j ϵt,ji, (23)

ϵt,ji = Dt,jj ϵt-1,ji + Dt,jj f ∘ xi,t,

where xt ∈ R is a scalar, ϵt,ji ∈ RHd×H is a block matrix with H × H blocks where each ϵt,ji ∈ Rd×1, and ⟨(cid:6),(cid:6)⟩: Rd×1 × Rd×1 → R denotes the inner product.

Similarly, for pp-prop, Eq. (24) becomes:

∇θ ji L ≈ ∑t=T ∂Lt/∂ht,j ∘ ϵt f,j ⟨ϵt x,i⟩, (24)

ϵt f,j = αDt,jj f ϵt-1 f,j + (1 - α)Dt,jj f,

where ϵt f,j ∈ RHd×1 is a block vector with each ϵt f,j ∈ Rd×1, and ϵt x,i ∈ R tracks the presynaptic eligibility trace of neuron i.

In summary, extending the derivations from d = 1 to d > 1 simply replaces scalars with blocks and element-wise multiplications with block-wise multiplications. The online learning framework remains structurally identical, while gaining the ability to represent richer neuron dynamics and more complex temporal dependencies.

Learning signals in deep recurrent layers. At time t, we compute the learning signal ∂Lt/∂ht,l at layer l using backpropagation through the stacked hidden layers. To maintain linear memory complexity, we consider two approaches based on when the top-down learning signal reaches layer l.

The first approach uses the learning signal arriving at layer l at time t, capturing instantaneous dependencies across hierarchical layers:

∇θ l L = ∑t∈T ∂Lt/∂ht,l ∘ ϵt,l. (25)

The second approach uses the learning signal arriving at layer l at time t-1, capturing dependencies across time:

∇θ l L = ∑t∈T ∂Lt/∂ht,l-1 ∘ ϵt,l-1. (26)

Experimental details for cognitive tasks
Surrogate gradient function. The spike generation function (Supplementary Eq. 36) uses a Heaviside step function with a transition at the firing threshold vth. Since this function is non-differentiable, we employ a surrogate gradient approach53 to enable gradient-based training.

During the forward pass, spikes are generated using the Heaviside function:

zt = spike(x) = H(vt - vth),

where x = vt - vth. During the backward pass, we approximate the derivative using a triangular surrogate3:

spike'(x) = ReLU(α ⋅ (width - |x|)),

where α = 0.3 controls the gradient amplitude, and width = 1.0 controls the gradient width. This produces a triangular function centered at x = 0, with peak value α ⋅ width, and zero gradient for |x| > width.

Weight initialization. For the networks defined in Supplementary Eqs. 70–78, we initialize input, recurrent, and readout weights using a scaled Gaussian distribution:

Wji ∼ N(0, s/sqrt(Nin)),

where Wji is the weight from neuron i to neuron j, Nin is the number of presynaptic neurons, and s is a scaling factor controlling the overall weight magnitude. This initialization helps keep activation and gradient variances well-behaved, improving training stability.

For networks with explicit excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) separation (Supplementary Eq. 81), we use the same scaled Gaussian distribution but enforce non-negative weights:

Wji ∼ |N(0, s/sqrt(Nin))|.

Taking the absolute value ensures that excitatory neurons produce only positive outgoing weights and inhibitory neurons only negative ones, in accordance with Dale’s principle. This constraint preserves the desired biological structure while maintaining an appropriate weight scale.

Delayed match-to-sample task. We tested the long-term dependency learning capability of our algorithms by training a recurrent spiking network (Supplementary Eq. 73) on a delayed match-to-sample (DMTS) task27,54. This task comprises four phases: fixation, sample, delay, and test (Supplementary Fig. 17). During the sample and test phases, one of eight motion directions is presented for 500 ms. The delay phase (>1000 ms) separates the sample and test, during which no stimulus is presented. The network must maintain sample direction information across this delay, then determine whether the test stimulus matches. A leaky readout layer processes network activity during the test phase to produce the match/non-match decision.

The network receives input from 100 motion-direction-tuned neurons covering 360 degrees, simulating direction-selective cells in the visual cortex. The firing rate ut,i of input neuron i follows a von Mises tuning curve:

ut,i = Aexp(κ(cos(θ - θi,pref) - 1)), (27)

where θ is the stimulus direction, θi,pref is the preferred direction of neuron i, κ = 2.0 is the concentration parameter, and A = 40 Hz is the maximum firing rate. A constant background rate rbg = 1 Hz is maintained throughout all task phases. Spike trains are generated via a Poisson process with rate ut,i + rbg during stimulus periods and rbg otherwise (Supplementary Fig. 17).

Evidence accumulation task. Evidence accumulation is a fundamental paradigm for studying decision-making mechanisms. We adopted a task design from Morcos et al.41, where a mouse navigates a virtual T-maze and encounters visual cues on both sides (Fig. 5A). At the T-junction, the mouse must choose the direction corresponding to the majority of cues, requiring it to accumulate and retain evidence from each side until the decision point.

We simulated this task using 100 input neurons divided into four groups of 25 neurons each: left-cue encoding, right-cue encoding, recall-cue encoding, and background noise. Cue and recall stimuli are modeled as Poisson spike trains at 40 Hz, with each stimulus lasting 150 ms separated by 50 ms intervals. Background neurons fire at a constant 10 Hz throughout the trial. Following the cue presentation, a 1000 ms delay precedes the recall stimulus (Fig. 5A).

The leaky rate readout. The networks in Fig. 4E–H and Fig. 5 use a leaky readout mechanism with output neurons corresponding to each task label. These neurons receive linear projections from the recurrent layer and perform decoding based on membrane potentials rather than spikes.

The readout dynamics follow:

τout dy/dt = -y + Wout rrec + bout, (28)

where y is the output neuron activity, τout is the time constant, Wout and bout are the weights and bias, and rrec concatenates membrane potentials and spike activities from recurrent neurons.

Resting-state whole-brain in vivo imaging data
Our Drosophila whole-brain in vivo imaging data derive from experimental studies by Mann et al. (2017)17 and Turner et al. (2021)18. They recorded resting-state neural activity in Drosophila using whole-brain calcium imaging of adult flies expressing the calcium-sensitive fluorescent protein GCaMP6s and membrane-tagged tdTomato. The central brain was exposed and imaged in vivo using resonant scanning two-photon microscopy at 3 μm isotropic resolution with 1.2 Hz temporal sampling for approximately 17 minutes per recording. They aligned functional data to a standard brain atlas using CMTK computational tools and defined regions of interest (ROIs) based on anatomical boundaries from established atlases (Ito or Branson). From each ROI, they extracted fluorescence time series, applied high-pass filtering to remove slow drift, and converted signals to ΔF/F measurements. The exemplary traces of recording ΔF/F can be obtained in Fig. 6A. We used deconvolution methods to transform these calcium imaging data into the neuropil firing rate (Supplementary Note H).

Whole-brain Drosophila connectome-constrained model
Network architecture. The whole-brain spiking network contains over 125,000 neurons and 50 million synaptic connections, organized into interconnected components (Supplementary Fig. 18).

Training operates on two distinct timescales. The neuropil firing rate is sampled at 1.2 Hz, with each datapoint representing approximately 833 ms of biological time. We denote the neuropil firing rate at timestep T as NeuropilFRT. In contrast, the spiking network simulation uses a 0.2 ms timestep, yielding 4165 simulation steps per neuropil sample. We use t for simulation time and T for neuropil time.

At each simulation step t, the network processes both recurrent input It (see Recurrent encoder) and external input It derived from the previous neuropil firing rate (see Input encoder). The recurrent connectivity matrix W is derived from the FlyWire connectome15. After completing all simulation steps within a neuropil time window, we compute each neuron’s firing rate and transform it to neuropil-level firing rates for comparison with experimental data (see Neuropil firing rate readout).

Network dynamics. The network dynamics follow the LIF model developed by Shiu et al.16:

τmbr dv i/dt = -g i(v i - Vresting) + Iext, (29)

dg i/dt = -g i/τrec + Irec, (30)

where v i is the membrane potential and g i is the synaptic conductance of neuron i. When v i ≥ Vthreshold, the neuron fires and resets to Vreset, followed by a refractory period of Trefractory = 2.2 ms.

Biophysical parameters are set to physiologically realistic values: Vresting = Vreset = -52 mV, Vthreshold = -45 mV, Rmbr = 10 KΩ ⋅ cm2, Cmbr = 2 μF ⋅ cm-2, Tmbr = 20 ms, τ = 5 ms, Tdelay = 1.8 ms, and Wsyn = 0.275 mV.

Input encoder. The input encoder transforms neuropil firing rates from the previous time step into background input for the current time step. Specifically, the encoder takes the neuropil firing rate at timestep T-1 (denoted as NeuropilFRT-1) and generates the external input IT ext for each neuron at timestep T. All firing rates are measured in Hz. During the T-th neuropil timestep, neuron i receives Poisson spike noise based on the transformed firing rate FRT ext,i. To capture temporal dependencies between different time steps, we employ a gated recurrent unit (GRU)55 followed by a linear transformation as the encoder for the Drosophila whole brain model. The transformation is given by:

FRT ext = Linear(GRU(NeuropilFRT-1)) (31)

Then, the neuropil-time-scale firing rate drives Poisson spike noise added to the membrane potential:

Iext(t) = ∑j δ(t - tj) wi, (32)

where δ(t-tj) represents Poisson spike times and wi is the learned synaptic weight for neuron i. During training, NeuropilFRT corresponds to experimental recordings; during inference, it refers to the simulated firing rate at the last step.

Recurrent encoder. The recurrent input to neuron i at time t is:

Irec,i(t) = ∑j δ(t - tspk j) wj,i (33)

The synaptic weight wj,i is computed by scaling the FlyWire connectome strength15 with a sign factor (+1 for excitatory, -1 for inhibitory) and the baseline synaptic weight Wsyn.

Neuropil firing rate readout. Each neuropil’s firing rate is computed as a weighted average of its constituent neurons’ firing rates. Because neuron density and connectivity vary across neuropils, simple averaging would distort the measured activity. Instead, each neuron is weighted by its normalized synaptic projection count into that neuropil:

SimFRi = ∑j rj wj,i / ∑j wj,i (34)

where rj is the firing rate of neuron j and wj,i is its normalized synaptic projection weight to neuropil i, obtained from the FlyWire connectome15. This weighting emphasizes neurons with stronger anatomical influence, yielding a more biologically faithful estimate of neuropil activity.

Robust automatic online learning through the Jaxpr compilation
The backpropagation algorithm owes much of its success to automatic differentiation frameworks like PyTorch21 and TensorFlow22, which abstract away gradient computation details. Inspired by this, we developed a general programming interface for online learning in SNNs that automatically derives eligibility traces and learning signals. Users need only define network dynamics and architecture; the interface handles all online learning computations.

Developing this framework requires addressing three challenges: (1) deriving eligibility traces, (2) generating learning signals, and (3) computing parameter gradients. We leverage Jaxpr, JAX’s intermediate representation56, to inspect computation graphs using abstract symbols. This enables us to analyze user-defined models and regenerate code that encompasses both state evolution and online learning, a process we call “online learning compilation”. During online learning compilation, we can also perform comprehensive optimizations to maximize computational performance and minimize the memory footprint that we need (see Supplementary Note I).

Deriving eligibility traces. Automatic derivation of eligibility traces involves three steps.

First, we analyze hidden state groups h l = [v1, ..., vd] within each recurrent layer to determine how state variables interact. This yields the block diagonal matrices Dt l for each layer l ∈ {1,…,L}.

Second, we analyze weight-to-hidden relationships ∂ht/∂θt by enumerating the computation graph to determine which hidden state each parameter connects to. This yields the block diagonal matrix Dt f.

Third, we generate the Jaxpr representation of eligibility traces (Eqs. (4)–(8)) based on the above analysis.

Generating learning signals. We use backpropagation through deep layers to generate learning signals (Eq. (2)).

Computing Eq. (25) need to save the gradients of intermediate variables. This is not allowed directly in JAX since hidden states computed within a function cannot be passed as function parameters. To overcome this, we employ a perturbation trick: we add zero perturbation δ to each hidden state, yielding ht + δ. By treating this perturbation as a function parameter, we exploit the equivalence ∂Lt/∂ht = ∂Lt/∂(ht + δ). We then use JAX’s jax.vjp interface to compute the ∂Lt/∂(ht + δ) derivatives and extract the result as a Jaxpr representation.

For computing Eq. (26), we directly take derivatives of hidden states at the previous time step ∂Lt/∂ht-1.

Computing parameter gradients. We integrate eligibility traces and learning signals using JAX’s jax.custom_vjp to define a custom vector-Jacobian product rule. This enables weight gradients to be accessed via standard interfaces like jax.grad while internally applying our online learning rules.

Our implementation defines two functions: (1) a forward pass function that computes network propagation and eligibility traces, and (2) a backward pass function that computes learning signals and parameter gradients by combining eligibility traces with learning signals. See Listing S4 for an example.

The resulting interface requires only two lines of code:

# define online computation using the pp-prop algorithm
model = braintrace.pp_prop(net, decay_or_rank=0.98)
# define online computation using the D-RTRL algorithm
model = braintrace.D_RTRL(net)
# compile the online learning graph using the input data
model.compile_graph(inputs)

### Reviewer 3

Wang et al. introduce BrainScale, a framework for automatic differentiation for spiking networks, that internally uses an
algorithm called ES-D-RTRL to compute gradients for spiking networks. ES-D-RTRL is an application of approximate
diagonalized real-time recurrent learning (RTRL) to spiking neural networks. Wang et al. present some first results of this
new framework to demonstrate its functionality. The manuscript contains a number of nice concepts and is presented clearly.
However, BrainScale lacks novelty over existing methods and should discuss prior work more exhaustively.
The need for software tools to automate the process of constructing large and complex spiking networks and suitable
learning mechanisms has been extensively explored in prior work, e.g. early on by Chris Eliasmith's Nengo framework [7],
Eshraghian et al., [2] or jaxsnn, Müller et al. 2024 [3], to name just a few (see e.g. Pietrzak et al. 2023 [1] for a review).
Clearly, BrainScales solves many problems in a different way, but in the light of this extensive prior work, the introduction
and discussion overstate the novelty of the proposed framework. Relevant related work should be cited alongside a
clarification of what is novel in BrainScale.
The idea of using RTRL for spiking neurons is not new either. Note that even e-Prop (ref. 6) is a simple variant of spiking
RTRL. Mingqing Xiao et al. had a paper in NeurIPS two years ago that is conceptually very similar to the work presented
here. It is also cited in the abstract of the manuscript (ref. 82). They used a leaky-integrate-and-fire neuron model and derived
an approximate version of RTRL. The approximation used a very similar diagonalization to achieve linear scaling (as done
in the current manuscript). They show theoretical and experimental results for recurrent and feedforward networks. LIF
neurons are very similar to the exponential synaptic response kernel that is used in the derivation of ES-D-RTRL. In the light
of this similarity, the manuscript seems a bit unfair towards ref. 82. It is only cited in the abstract in the statement "... or use
oversimplified models [82], failing to capture the intricate brain dynamics." What exactly are the intricate brain dynamics that
BrainScale can capture and prior methods failed to address? A detailed side-by-side comparison would be in need here.
Also the simulation results reported here are misleading in the sense that they miss a fair comparison with state-of-the art.
94% test accuracy on DVS gesture dataset is not state of the art. Modern machine learning method achieve 100% on this
data set, see: [4]. Why this gap? Should be discussed. Furthermore, Xiao et al. [ref 82] also reported superior results on DVS
gesture dataset (>96%). Please include and discuss their result and compare the difference in detail, given the relevance of
this work (see also comment above). They also presented compelling results for the more complex cifar 10 and 100 data
sets, among others. Would be interesting to include those as well here. Also on Spiking speech commands much better
results have been reported, e.g. [5, 6]. Why this gap? Please discuss. Furthermore, the comparison with BPTT without
surrogate is not very meaningful, since BPTT for spiking neurons in that case simply doesn't work. Also, why stop learning in
Fig.5E,F at 95%? What is significant about this number, and how would convergence behave after reaching that point?

To address this gap, the revised manuscript now explicitly acknowledges this prior

contribution lies in tackling a critical yet often overlooked issue in the field of
online learning algorithms: the lack of a systematic summary and formal definition of

generalize to more complex neural dynamics. While more general algorithms such as e-

applying online learning algorithms to a broader range of network structures and
dynamic systems. The clear presentation of these model boundaries is a cornerstone of
the extensibility and generalizability of our framework, and it plays a foundational
role in advancing the application of online learning methods to complex neural
modeling and neuromorphic systems. Moreover, this formalism will offer valuable
guidance for the future design and refinement of online learning algorithms.

We are indeed aware that the name BrainScale bears some resemblance to the existing
hardware platform BrainScaleS (brain-inspired multi-scale computation in
neuromorphic hybrid systems). This similarity has prompted several rounds of internal
discussion and exploration of alternative naming options. However, after careful
consideration, we believe that BrainScale remains the most appropriate name to
capture the core vision and technical essence of our system.
First, BrainScale is tightly coupled with the broader Brain Modeling Ecosystem (htt
ps:  brainmodeling.readthedocs.io/) we are building. This ecosystem includes tools
such as BrainUnit, which provides physical unit support; BrainEvent, which implements
event-driven computing capabilities; BrainCell, which enables biologically detailed
neuron modeling; and BrainState, which supports state-based compilation. BrainScale
plays a critical role in this ecosystem by delivering scalable online learning
capabilities, thereby completing the stack needed for advanced brain dynamics
modeling.
Second, the name BrainScale directly reflects the central objective of our system:
enabling scalability in brain dynamics simulation and modeling during training. The
term concisely encapsulates our project's overarching mission, supporting the scaling
up of brain-inspired computational models. Concepts such as "scale up" and
"scalability" are not auxiliary features but are foundational to our work. As such,
the name BrainScale clearly and efficiently communicates this core innovation.
Moreover, while the names are similar, BrainScale and BrainScaleS differ
significantly in scope and technological focus. BrainScaleS is renowned for its
contributions to neuromorphic hardware. In contrast, BrainScale operates at the
software and algorithmic levels, representing a fundamentally different layer of the
technology stack. This distinction highlights the divergence in application domains
and intended usage between the two systems.
That said, we deeply value feedback from the community and will continue to assess
the appropriateness and potential impact of our naming choices to ensure they do not
inadvertently cause confusion or undermine existing contributions.

Thanks for the careful comment.
We agree that the original phrasing  “Eq. 1 is capable of modeling the exact dynamics
of realistic brain networks under …”  was imprecise and potentially misleading.
Our intended meaning was to highlight the consistency between simplified models (such
as those based on the AlignPre and AlignPost abstractions) and the original, non-
simplified dynamical models. Specifically, we meant that the simplified formulation
used in Eq. 1 preserves key dynamical features when compared to the original,
continuous-time models, thereby enabling faithful simulation under certain
assumptions.
However, even with such consistency, Eq. 1 remains a discrete-time approximation and
therefore cannot be said to model the exact dynamics in the strict mathematical or
biological sense. A more accurate description is that, under a given time step and
specific numerical integration scheme, Eq. 1 provides a numerically faithful
approximation to the solutions of differential equation-based neuron models. It
effectively captures the essential dynamical behavior of these models, but only
within the limits of its discretization.
Also, the term "exact dynamics of brain networks" is problematic in itself, as the
dynamics of real brain networks are highly complex and inherently uncertain. No
mathematical model can claim to capture them with absolute precision; all modeling
efforts are necessarily performed at a particular level of abstraction.
To improve the rigor and clarity of the manuscript, we have removed the old phrase
from the revised version. Instead, we now explicitly emphasize the rationale behind
the use of the simplified discrete form (see Lines 86-94) and discuss its advantages
more clearly (see Lines 95-99).

Thanks for this question.
In our experiments on brain simulation models (Figure 4E–H, Figure 5), the outputs of
the recurrent layers are based on membrane potentials rather than spike events. This
contrasts with the brain-inspired computational models (Figure I–L, Table 1), where
the outputs are discrete spike trains. The main reason for this design choice is that
spikes are extremely sparse in realistic neuronal dynamics, whereas membrane
potentials provide richer and more continuous information, making them more suitable
as decoding targets in these models. Moreover, since it remains unclear how the brain
decodes information, we opted to use membrane potential as the decoding target
(Supplementary Note I.5). Nevertheless, decoding based on spikes can also
successfully accomplish this task, but converges slowly (data not shown).
Although the decoding is based on membrane potentials, neuronal spikes play a
critical role in the internal forward dynamics, since spikes are still used to
mediate synaptic interactions. Therefore, it is not a trivial thing that BPTT without
surrogate gradients cannot successfully train this tasks (as shown in Fig. 4F and
Fig. 5C).

We appreciate your insight regarding the potential comparison with ANN-SNN conversion

following reasons:
First, our team's expertise and focus lie in the area of online learning for SNNs,
rather than offline training or ANN-SNN conversion methods. Incorporating and
evaluating conversion-based baselines would require significant additional effort,
including non-trivial reimplementation and tuning. We lack in-house expertise with
ANN-SNN conversion protocols, and reproducing these experiments would require a
substantial investment of time and resources  far exceeding the eight months already
devoted to the present revision.
Second, our primary contribution lies in co-optimizing algorithms and frameworks for
scalable online SNN learning. Therefore, we compare against state-of-the-art online
learning methods (see OSTL, E-prop, ETLP, OSTTP, OTPE, S-TLLR, FPTT, and OTTT in
Table 1) that share the same learning constraints and objectives. Including ANN-SNN
conversion would introduce a different class of methods that, while valuable,
addresses distinct research questions related to knowledge transfer rather than
online adaptation.

We appreciate the suggestion to compare memory usage with STDP. As the reviewer
noted, STDP requires memory for pre- and post-synaptic traces, which is
comparable to the memory footprint of our ES-D-RTRL algorithm. However, the key
distinction lies in computational cost: STDP requires weight updates at every time
step, while ES-D-RTRL performs updates only when a learning signal is delivered. This
leads to significantly lower computational overhead during online learning,
especially for long sequences or sparse feedback settings.

approximates gradient-based credit assignment. It achieves strong task performance
while maintaining linear memory complexity  matching STDP in efficiency but with
significantly greater generalization power. See supplementary Note M.

online learning rules into efficient, hardware-compatible implementations. To

1. The contribution and novelty
While the general idea of applying RTRL to spiking neurons has been explored before,
our key contribution lies in deriving a theoretically principled, event-driven RTRL
algorithm (ES-D-RTRL) for general SNN models that achieves linear memory complexity .
This extends beyond previous approximations in both scope and rigor.
In contrast to OTTT (Xiao et al.), our algorithm:
(A) Generalization to arbitrary neuron & synapse models
– Xiao et al. (OTTT) focus on LIF neurons with single exponential synapses. In ES-D-
RTRL, we derive an online gradient for any combination of neuron and synapse dynamics
—LIF, ALIF, conductance-based channels, multi-exponential kernels, adaptation, reset
and refractoriness—without altering the core algorithm.
– This breadth is crucial for brain simulation and neuromorphic applications, where
diverse biophysical mechanisms interplay.
(B) Exact O(n) memory & computation with theoretical guarantees
– OTTT reduces complexity by dropping post-synaptic reset/adaptation terms from the
surrogate gradient and then empirically showing negligible impact on small networks.
– In contrast, ES-D-RTRL performs a rank-1 decomposition of the full Jacobian,
including all post-synaptic dynamics, and reformulates the double sum as a product of
two vector sums. This yields true memory and per-step updates with
rigorous bounds on gradient fidelity and convergence.

3. Exponential kernel vs. LIF dynamics
Regarding the similarity between LIF neurons and the exponential kernel in Eq. (7):
While both may involve exponential terms, their roles are fundamentally different. In
OTTT, the exponential kernel arises directly from the LIF neuron dynamics and is
tightly coupled to the structure of the neuron model. In contrast, our use of
exponential kernels in Eq. (7) is part of a generic temporal filter applied to the
output spikes, and is independent of the internal dynamics of the neuron model (e.g.,
LIF, ALIF, Izhikevich, Hodgkin–Huxley, etc).
Moreover, the influence of neuron dynamics in our method is captured by Eq. (8),
which models post-synaptic responses. This separation of spike filtering (Eq. 7) and
dynamical response (Eq. 8) allows our framework to generalize well across neuron and
synapse types.

2. Model architecture and fairness of results
In the initial submission, the observed performance gap was primarily due to the use
of simple network architectures and neuron models, which were intentionally selected
to ensure clarity and controlled analysis rather than to maximize performance. In the
revised version, we have incorporated more advanced neuron models (e.g., adLIF,
RadLIF, and EGRU) and demonstrated that our learning algorithm scales effectively,
achieving over 97% accuracy on DVS Gesture and over 93% on SHD. These improvements

online learning method supports high-performance training of advanced spiking network
architectures.
The reviewer noted that modern machine learning methods achieve 100% on this
dataset, see: [4]. The referenced work employs deep state-space models (SSMs) for
processing neuromorphic datasets. While SSMs have shown strong performance on tasks
involving long-term sequential dependencies, they are rate-based rather than spiking
models, and thus fall outside the scope of this manuscript. Moreover, such models are
incompatible with the ES-D-RTRL framework we explore. For these reasons, we did not
evaluate SSMs within our online learning system.
Finally, our current evaluations  covering a variety of SNN models and benchmarks  
already demonstrate the strong performance of our learning algorithms. Therefore, we
chose not to include additional datasets such as CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, which are
beyond the primary focus of this study.
